common_name: Bellflower Solomon's Seal (Dwarf Running Chinese Solomon's Seal)

planting.note: Plant rhizome sections in spring or fall in humus-rich, moist, well-drained woodland soil in full to dappled shade; this dwarf Chinese species spreads steadily by slender rhizomes to knit into a low colony rather than forming a single upright clump.

directions: Set rhizome divisions an inch or two deep in cool, humus-rich soil that stays evenly moist, and let the plant wander to form a loose groundcover beneath deciduous trees. Compared to the taller border Solomon's seals, this Sichuan and Yunnan native stays noticeably shorter, carrying wide, pendant, bell-shaped white flowers with green tips in late spring beneath narrower, more pointed leaves than P. odoratum. Top-dress annually with leaf mold to replicate its native forest-floor conditions, and divide congested patches in early spring only when you want to slow its spread rather than out of necessity, since it resents excessive disturbance. Use it as a running companion to ferns and trilliums where a taller Solomon's seal would overwhelm the scene.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew Science)
Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden

common_name: Pratt's Solomon's Seal (Whorled-Leaf Dwarf Chinese Solomon's Seal)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled to full shade; this compact western Chinese species prefers cooler root conditions and resents waterlogging more than the common garden Solomon's seals.

directions: Give this diminutive Sichuan native a cool, well-drained woodland or rock-garden pocket with humus-rich soil, since it is one of the smallest Solomon's seals in cultivation and can be lost among coarser companions. Narrow leaves ring the thin, wiry stems in tiers, echoing the larger whorled-leaf P. verticillatum but on a much reduced scale, with small greenish-white bells dangling below each whorl in late spring. Keep it out of hot, humid summer sun and avoid heavy, wet clay, mulching lightly with leaf litter to mimic the cool montane forest floor it comes from. Because it stays so compact, it is best grown as a specimen near a path edge or in a trough rather than massed with vigorous spreaders.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew Science)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in humus-rich, moist, well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade; clumps expand slowly and benefit from an annual mulch of leaf mold.

directions: This lesser-grown Chinese woodlander from Yunnan and Guizhou carries clusters of narrow, pale greenish-yellow bells in spring at the tips of arching, purple-tinged stems, followed by dark berries in late summer. It clumps more tightly than the widely offered Disporum cantoniense selections, making it a good choice for a shaded border where a running habit is unwanted, and its purplish new growth adds early-season color before the leaves fully green up. Plant in consistently moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil beneath high shade, and protect from late spring frost while shoots are still emerging. Divide congested clumps in early spring only when needed, since established plants resent frequent disturbance.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew Science)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in deep, fertile, constantly moist soil in partial shade, sheltered from drying wind; 'Buckland Beauty' holds a bronze cast to its pinnate foliage longer into the season than plain-green forms.

directions: Plant in deep, humus-rich, reliably moist soil at a pond margin or streamside where the bold, deeply veined leaves will never dry out, since scorched leaf tips are the main setback for this genus in a drier border. 'Buckland Beauty' produces broad, bronze-flushed pinnate foliage on sturdy upright stems, topped in early to midsummer by tall, feathery plumes of clear pink, star-shaped flowers that stand well above the leaves. Shelter the planting from strong wind, which can tatter the large leaflets, and mulch heavily each spring to conserve the constant moisture this species demands. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in early spring to keep the foliage dense and the flower display strong.

common_name: Spanish Cross Foamflower (Dark Cross-Marked Cut-Leaf Tiarella)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or early fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in shade to part shade; the deeply cut foliage is marked with a bold dark central pattern that intensifies in cooler weather.

directions: This Terra Nova introduction carries deeply, sharply cut leaves marked with a bold, dark cross-shaped blotch radiating from the center of each leaf, a pattern that deepens to near-black in fall and winter cold. Fluffy spikes of small white to pale pink star-shaped flowers rise above the foliage clump in spring, drawing early bees before the surrounding woodland canopy leafs out. Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to part shade, and mulch with shredded leaves to keep roots cool through summer. Divide congested clumps in early spring or immediately after flowering to maintain a tight, well-marked foliage mound.

common_name: Azurea Lungwort (Unspotted Deep Blue Narrow-Leaf Pulmonaria)

planting.note: Divide clumps in early spring or right after flowering, replanting in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; 'Azurea' carries plain unspotted green leaves rather than the silver mottling typical of most garden Pulmonaria.

directions: One of the oldest named Pulmonaria selections still in cultivation, 'Azurea' produces clear, intensely deep blue funnel-shaped flowers in early spring, a shade richer and truer than the pink-fading-to-blue displays of most spotted-leaf types. Its narrow, plain green leaves lack silver marbling entirely, giving the clump a simpler, more uniform texture once the flowers fade in late spring. Plant in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where it spreads gently into a low mat over a few seasons. Divide every three to four years in early spring to refresh vigor and increase the planting.

planting.note: Divide clumps in early spring or right after flowering, replanting in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; 'Redstart' begins flowering earlier than most Pulmonaria, sometimes as winter is still ending.

directions: Like the species it derives from, 'Redstart' carries plain matte-green, unspotted leaves, but it is grown chiefly for flowers that open an unusually vivid coral-red rather than the typical pink-to-blue progression of most Pulmonaria. Blooms appear remarkably early, often opening while snow or hard frost still lingers, giving pollinators and gardeners alike one of the first splashes of color in the shade garden. Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and shear back tattered foliage after flowering to encourage a fresh, mildew-resistant summer mound. Divide congested clumps every few years in early spring to maintain flowering vigor.

planting.note: Divide clumps in early spring or right after flowering, replanting in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; 'Argentea' is among the oldest selections grown for leaves that read almost entirely silver rather than spotted.

directions: An older English selection that predates the heavily marketed near-solid-silver Pulmonaria of recent decades, 'Argentea' bears broad, felted leaves so densely overlaid with silver that only a thin band of green shows at the margin and along the veins. Clusters of funnel-shaped flowers open pink from the bud and mature to violet-blue in early spring, appearing before the foliage has fully expanded to its summer size. Plant in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and water during dry spells since the broad leaves wilt quickly under drought stress. Cut back tired summer foliage to refresh the clump and keep the silvering bright for the following spring.

common_name: Luchu Leopard Plant (Dwarf Ryukyu Island Farfugium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in part sun to full shade after the last frost; this naturally dwarf botanical variety from the Ryukyu Islands stays smaller in every part than the typical species.

directions: Native to Okinawa and neighboring Ryukyu Islands, this compact botanical variety is the wild parent behind several of the smaller-growing Farfugium cultivars in trade, itself forming a tidy rosette of rounded, glossy leaves well under half the size of the mainland species. Mustard-yellow daisy flowers rise on short stalks above the foliage in autumn, extending seasonal interest once most other shade perennials have finished. Site it in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in part sun to full shade, mulching to keep roots cool through summer heat, and grow it in a container or raised bed in colder zones where winters exceed its hardiness. Its reduced scale makes it a useful edging or rock-garden accent where the full-sized species would be too bulky.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden
